```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
options(width = 90, digits = 4)
```

`emss` estimates cut scores with **embedded standard setting** (ESS; Lewis &
Cook, 2020). Panelists align each item to the performance level whose
descriptor it matches. `emss` then places each cut score where the items'
locations on the reporting scale agree best with those alignments. This
article covers the basic workflow. [How embedded standard setting
works](ess-method.html) explains what is computed and why, with a worked
example and the underlying mathematics.

# Installation

```{r}
#| eval: false
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("sooyongl/emss")
```

```{r}
library(emss)
```

# What `emss` needs

| Input | Required | One row per | Main columns |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Ratings | yes | panelist × item (× round) | grade, panelist, item ID, aligned level; optional table and round |
| Items | yes | item | grade, item ID, one or more location columns (e.g., `RP67`); optional `Domain`, `Order_of_Difficulty` |
| Setup | optional | grade | `Level Options` (level labels, lowest to highest), `SD`, `EC` |
| Examinee scores | optional | grade × score | grade, `Score`, `Freq` (long format), for impact data |

The example of data structure can be found below in a simulated study section.

The location is each item's position on the reporting scale, typically a
response-probability location such as RP67 (for more details, see [Item Location](item-locations.html)). The item table may hold several
location columns. The `location` argument of `emstans()` picks one.

# A simulated study

`genFakeDataSet()` simulates a complete study: here three grades, two tables
of four panelists each, 40 items per grade, three performance levels, and
three content domains.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
set.seed(7)
sim <- genFakeDataSet(ngca = 3, ntable = 2, npanelist = 4, cor_val = 0.7, nlevel = 3,
                      sdinp = 1, ecinp = 0, n = 40, 300, 500,
                      domains = c("Number", "Algebra", "Geometry"))
names(sim)
head(sim$setup, 3)
head(sim$panelist, 4)
head(sim$rating, 5)
head(sim$item_data, 5)
head(sim$examineedata_data, 10)
```

`sdinp` (SD in the `sim$setup`) and `ecinp` (EC in the `sim$setup`) must be named here: the unnamed values that follow `n`
(300 and 500) are the range of the item locations.

# Estimating cut scores

```{r}
#| label: fit
res <- emstans(data = sim, location = "Loc_RP50")
res
```

Each grade is analysed separately. For each one, `emss` estimates a cut score
for every panelist and for the **modal** alignment across panelists, per
table and for all tables together. The printed cut scores are the modal
cuts for all tables. Each cut is named by the level it opens: `Level2` is
the lowest score in Level 2.

The main options are:

| Argument | Values |
|:--|:--|
| `location` | name of the item location column, such as `"RP67"` |
| `method` | `"weight"` (ESS-Weight, default) or `"count"` (ESS-Count) |
| `grades` | grades to analyse, by name or position (default: all) |
| `by_domain`, `domains` | also analyse each content domain, or the listed ones |
| `smooth` | `TRUE` to take cuts from a GAM-smoothed inconsistency profile |

# Results

`summary()` puts the modal cut next to the median and average of the
panelists' cuts, and adds the agreement between aligned and empirical
levels:

```{r}
#| label: summary
summary(res)
```

`extract()` returns the results as data frames, with level labels as
ordered factors:

```{r}
#| label: extract
extract(res, "cutscore")                    # modal cut scores, one vector per unit
ind <- extract(res, "individual")           # panelist, modal, median, average
head(ind$panelist[, c("unit", "table", "panelist", "correlation", "cut_level",
                      "page", "cut_score")])
extract(res, "detailed")$agreement          # agreement and weighted kappa
im <- extract(res, "summary")               # impact data
im[im$unit == "M1-All", ]
rv <- extract(res, "review")                # items whose alignment disagrees with the cuts
head(rv[rv$status != "Consistent", c("unit", "item_id", "aligned", "operational",
                                     "location", "distance", "status")])
```

Other options are `"profile"` (the inconsistency profile of each unit) and
`"all"`.

# Plots

The inconsistency profile shows, for every candidate cut, how inconsistent
the items would be. The selected cuts are at the minima:

```{r}
#| label: plot-profile
plot(res, "profile", unit = "M1-All")
```

The impact plots show cut scores and examinee percentages across grades:

```{r}
#| label: plot-impact
#| fig-height: 3.5
p <- plot(res, "impact")
names(p)
p$cut_scores
p$percent_in
```

Both are ggplot objects and can be modified with the usual ggplot2 functions.

# Report

`report()` builds an interactive HTML report with every table and plot,
sections for individual cuts, agreement, impact and item review:

```{r}
#| eval: false
report(res)                       # opens in the viewer
report(res, what = "review")      # one section only
```

# More analyses

```{r}
#| label: more
# ESS-Count instead of ESS-Weight
emstans(data = sim, location = "Loc_RP50", method = "count")

# Each content domain as well as all items, for grade M1 only
res_dom <- emstans(data = sim, location = "Loc_RP50", grades = "M1", by_domain = TRUE)
extract(res_dom, "cutscore")
```

When the ratings contain several rounds, each round is analysed separately
and named accordingly, for example `M1-All Round 2`.

# Your own data

An EmStanS Excel workbook (sheets Setup, Panelists, Ratings, ItemMetaData,
ExamineeMetaData) can be passed directly:

```{r}
#| eval: false
res <- emstans("my_study.xlsx", location = "RP67")
```

Data frames or CSV files with other layouts go through `ess_data()`. Only
ratings and items are required. Level labels, SD and EC can come from a
setup table, from arguments, or both (arguments win). Columns whose names
differ from the defaults are mapped by name or position:

```{r}
#| eval: false
d <- ess_data(
  ratings   = "ratings.csv",
  items     = "items.csv",
  examinees = "scores.csv",                            # Grade, Score, Freq
  levels    = c("Basic", "Proficient", "Advanced"),    # lowest to highest
  sd        = 30,
  ec        = 5,
  columns   = list(ratings = list(panelist = "Rater", level = "Judgment"))
)
d                                  # what was read
res <- emstans(data = d, location = "RP67")
```

Level labels can also differ by grade, for example
`levels = list(G4 = c("E", "M", "L"), G5 = c("B", "P", "A"))`. Every table,
plot and report uses the labels, in level order.
